author: Vargas & Landry

Specimens have since been identified from Costa Rica via DNA barcoding. In 2019, Ann Hendrickson reared a moth from a cocoon found on Mimosa texana (A. Gray) Small (Fabaceae) in Edwards Co., TX. DNA barcoding showed 98.93% similarity with a Chilean specimen of C. yaroella and up to 99.85% similarity with the Costa Rican material. Unfortunately the TX specimen was destroyed and cannot be examined.

NAME: thermopsella
author: Chambers
NOTE: NOTE: This species was listed under Parectopa by Davis (in Hodges et al. 1983). Its identity is uncertain, since no confirmed specimens are known, but we transfer it to Micrurapteryx (n. comb.), based on the following: 1) the forewing has a white dorsal margin as in other Nearctic members of this genus; 2) the gracillariid leaf mines we have found on Thermopsis in CO (the type host and locality of M. thermopsella) look identical to those of M. occulta and unlike those of the Fabaceae-feeding Parectopa species (Eiseman 2022); and 3) in the USNM are two old, poor, inadequately labeled specimens of a Micrurapteryx distinct from M. occulta and M. salicifoliella, in the same tray with leaves of Thermopsis montana Nutt. from CO (but it is not known for certain that the moths came from these leaves). The identity of M. thermopsella will not be resolved until new specimens can be reared from Thermopsis (Fabaceae).

We interpret this as “clear evidence of an inadvertent error, such as a lapsus calami or a copyist's or printer's error,” which must be corrected according to ICZN Article 32.5.1.

NAME: robiniella
author: Clemens

NAME: quinquistrigella
author: Chambers
NOTE: NOTE: This species was listed in Acrocercops by Davis (in Hodges et al. 1983). CSE has reared adults that match the holotype externally (Eiseman 2022), and the larval biology together with the appearance of the adult indicate that G. quinquistrigella belongs in Ornixolinae rather than Acrocercopinae. The leafmine is similar to those of both acrocercopines and ornixolines, but the larva does not turn red in its final instar, as is said to be an apomorphy for Acrocercopinae (Kawahara et al. 2017). Since we are uncertain as to the correct generic placement of this species but it is clearly not an Acrocercops, we have provisionally placed it in Ornixolinae without a genus (n. comb.).

NAME: elongella
author: Linnaeus
NOTE: NOTE: This is a Palaearctic species and no confirmed specimens are known from NA. Pohl & Landry (in Pohl et al. 2018) stated that historical reports of C. elongella in NA refer to C. alnivorella, but the situation is more complicated. Busck (1904), for instance, concluded that alnicolella, alnivorella, fuscoochrella, nigristrigella, pulchella, ruptistrigella (misspelled “ruptostrigella” therein), sanguinella, and shastella (misspelled “shastaella” therein) all represented varieties of C. elongella, but three of these names (alnicolella, alnivorella, and pulchella) are currently recognized as valid. More recently, Passoa (1980) reported rearing C. elongella from Betula alleghaniensis Britton (Betulaceae) in NH. As noted by Eiseman (2022), Steven Passoa still has one of the specimens in his possession but it is missing its abdomen; an attempt by JFL to extract DNA failed, and its true identity is unclear.

Despite its name, C. populetorum feeds on Betula and Alnus spp. (Betulaceae) rather than on Populus spp. (Salicaceae).

NAME: ribesella
author: Chambers

It folds the leaves of the red wild currant so that the folded leaf resembles exactly one folded by Gelechia ribesella” (Chambers 1877). Chambers' (1875b) description of the latter species notes: “It folds the leaf downward from each side and the tip, and lives within the fold.” Clarke (1933) described adults of what he believed to be “Gracilaria ribesella”, which he reared from webbed leaves of Ribes bracteosum Douglas (Grossulariaceae) in WA, but Braun (1939) stated that his moths were actually Euhyponomeutoides gracilariella (Yponomeutidae). Because a Caloptilia on Ribes does exist in CO (Eiseman 2022), we retain this name as valid until adults can be reared and their identity determined.

author: Clarke

NAME: "Lithocolletis"
author: Hübner
NOTE: NOTE: This genus name is a synonym of Phyllonorycter, but is used here for provisional listing of an unplaced species.

NAME: lysimachiaeella
author: Chambers
NOTE: NOTE: The original description (Chambers 1875c) states only that the “larva is cylindrical and very small” and “makes a very small tentiform mine on the under side of the leaves of (Lysimachia lanceolata) the loosestrife. I have not succeeded in rearing it.” This species was listed in Phyllonorycter by Davis (in Hodges et al. 1983) based on the synonymy of Lithocolletis with that genus, but the adult remains unknown and no one since Chambers has reported finding gracillariid mines on L. lanceolata Walter (Primulaceae) or any other NA Primulaceae. Eiseman & Davis (2020) discussed the possibility that Chambers may have mistaken the feeding damage of a tortricid larva for the tentiform mine of a lithocolletine.

NAME: citrella
author: Stainton
NOTE: NOTE: This Asian citrus leaf miner was documented in FL by Heppner (1993) and is now established across the southern USA (Eiseman 2022).

NAME: magnoliella
author: Forbes
NOTE: NOTE: When Chambers (1880a) first introduced the name magnoliaeella he stated that this “species is known only in the larval and pupal states, and is probably identical with liriodendronella.” The species was not actually described in that publication — although he clearly was referring to the maker of the leaf mines on Magnolia (Magnoliaceae) he had discussed previously (Chambers 1871) — and thus it was listed as a nomen nudum by Davis (in Hodges et al. 1983), along with subsequent misspellings. The spelling “magnoliella” was first used by Dyar (1903), and later by Forbes (1923), who distinguished the adults of “P. liriodendrella Clemens” and “P. magnoliella Chambers” based on minor differences in wing pattern. Because this was the first description ever to accompany the name, magnoliella Forbes was listed as a valid species by Davis (in Hodges et al. 1983). No type specimen was designated since Forbes' intent was not to describe a new species. We agree with Darlington (1945) that Phyllocnistis adults reared from Magnolia and Liriodendron are indistinguishable, and magnoliella is hereby synonymized with P. liriodendronella (n. syn.). The synonymy is supported by the fact that CSE saw no sign of either “species” in his yard in MA for five years and then in 2019 mines appeared on both hosts simultaneously.

NAME: meliacella
author: Becker
NOTE: NOTE: This species, first described from Costa Rica, has since been found in FL (Heppner 2003).

NAME: vitifoliella
author: Chambers
NOTE: NOTE: We have not found consistent differences between adults of this species and P. vitegenella, and it was based on this presumed synonymy that the introduced European population (established around 1990 according to Kirichenko et al. (2018)) was identified as P. vitegenella (this being the older name). However, the leaf mines of the two are easily distinguished (Eiseman 2022), and in CSE's experience, mines on grape (Vitis spp.; Vitaceae) are always unambiguously one or the other. After reviewing European literature and websites concerning “P. vitegenella” and consulting with EJvN and Willem Ellis, it appears that only mines of the “vitifoliella” type have been found in Europe — strong evidence that the two species are in fact distinct.

NAME: cordiella
author: Busck

NAME: caryosphena
author: Meyrick
NOTE: NOTE: This species is closely related to the Palaearctic A. notana, and it has been listed in NA under that name as well as the notana synonyms ferrugana and tripunctana. We follow Karsholt et al. (2015) and treat the NA (including GR) populations as distinct from A. notana. Powell (in Hodges et al. 1983) listed caryosphena as well as notana (as tripunctana). Gilligan et al. (2020a) were not able to secure DNA, to determine the status of “A. notana” in NA. Acleris caryosphena has also been confused with A. arcticana, stemming from Meyrick's incorrect assumption about the hostplant in the original description. Meyrick described caryosphena from specimens collected among Betula spp. (Betulaceae) and Salix spp. (Salicaceae), and wrote “probably allied to hastiana and feeding on Salix”. That was incorrect, as A. caryosphena is a Betula-feeder, but it led future workers (including Brown 2005 and Pohl & Dombroskie, in: Pohl et al. 2018) to confuse it with the Salix-feeding A. arcticana.

(2020a) used DNA barcode data to confirm that the European A. logiana is a different taxon from the NA subspecies placidana, and they elevated placidana to species; this arrangement was partially reflected in Gilligan et al. (2018) based on a mistake in indicating placidana was a subspecies. Forbes (1923) used the European name niveana for this species.

NAME: disputabilis
author: Obraztsov
NOTE: NOTE: Historically the status of the species now recognized as A. disputabilis has been in dispute, and this is complicated by the fact that the type of ferruginiguttana is severely damaged. Obraztsov (1963b) described disputabilis, essentially as a replacement name for McDunnough's (1934) usage of the name ferruginiguttana, as a form of A. nigrolinea. Obraztsov makes clear that these do not exactly fit the original description of ferruginiguttana. Powell (1964) and Powell (in Hodges et al. 1983) had a broader concept of nigrolinea, and treated disputabilis and ferruginiguttana as synonyms of it. However, Powell & Opler (2009) follow Razowski (1966) and recognize A. disputabilis as distinct from A. nigrolinea; we tentatively follow the latter treatment here. Further work is warranted, as considerable DNA barcode variation is present in this group.

NAME: ferruginiguttana

NAME: Olethreutes

NOTE: NOTE: The taxonomy of the NA species of “Olethreutes” does not agree with European concepts. Although Brown (2005) made some progress toward resolving discrepancies in the generic assignments between the NA and European faunas in Olethreutes and related genera, nearly all of the NA species remaining in Olethreutes would be assigned to either Phiaris or Argyroploce as defined in the most recent European checklist (Aarvik 2017). We generally agree with the European treatment, and follow Aarvik. (2017) and other Eurasian sources (see individual species notes below) for Holarctic species, but we refrain from making extensive changes in generic assignment to the remaining NA species until there is a comprehensive worldwide revision of the group that includes all of these taxa.

NAME: trepidulum

NOTE: NOTE: This species is hereby recognized to be distinct from O. diallacta. Heinrich (1926) recognized that two species were confused under the name zelleriana, which was historically applied to this species as well as to the species now known as O. diallacta. This non-Betula-feeding (Betulaceae) species was treated erroneously as “Exartema zelleriana” by Kearfott in an unpublished manuscript; Heinrich recognized that it was distinct from Fernald's “zelleriana”, and described it as Exartema trepidulum.

NAME: diallacta
author: Meyrick
NOTE: NOTE: This name applies to the species that feeds on Betula (Betulaceae), which was confused with the species now known as O. trepidulum prior to Heinrich (1926); see details under that species. The name diallacta was proposed as a replacement name for zelleriana (Fernald, 1882). Fernald had proposed the name zelleriana for nitidana sensu Zeller, 1875, which Fernald had recognized as a species distinct from O. nitidana. However Fernald's name has no type or description, so it is a nomen nudum. Meyrick (1932) proposed Argyroploce diallacta as a replacement name, because A. zelleriana (Fernald, 1882) was preoccupied in Argyroploce by A. zelleriana (Erschoff, 1874) (now placed in Clepsis). Although the Fernald name is no longer preoccupied, as a nomen nudum it still requires a replacement, so O. diallacta becomes the valid name for this species.

NAME: pallida
author: Herrich-Schäffer
NOTE: REVISED NOTE: There is uncertainty about the separation of T. pallida and T. testacea, as well as uncertainty about the application of the names as they were described. It was suggested by Profant et al. (2010) that T. flexuosa is a synonym of T. pallida, but here we retain T. flexuosa as a separate species pending further research. The synonymy in Profant et al. (2010) was based on personal communication with ME, who via his curation of the NMNH collection showed specimens traditionally placed under each name blended together phenotypically and the genitalia could not be separated. Later ME (unpublished) found that DNA data, when compared with wing patterns, do not clearly differentiate the two taxa. That there are two taxa rather than one is suggested by Dyar (1896,1898), Wagner (2005) and Passoa (in Marquis et al. 2019), given there are two very different larval phenotypes, one tending to produce T. flexuosa of authors and the other T. pallida of authors. The original description of T. pallida by Herrich-Schäffer was only an illustration, one that matches what has been considered to be T. flexuosa by authors since. By priority, this would make the more marked phenotypes to be “true” T. pallida rather than those with little or no markings: the T. pallida of authors that followed. Tortricidia pallida of authors would be another taxon, perhaps T. flavula, which matches the less marked phenotype but is a darker, more vivid orange-brown. Pending further research, for expediency we treat the species as they have most recently been known.

NOTE: NOTE: GRP has determined that Hodges (1974) synonymized sciadopa with A. canadensis in error, and it is hereby moved into synonymy with Exaeretia ciniflonella (rev. syn.). Although we have not examined the type of sciadopa in the NHMUK, the original description by Meyrick (1920) and subsequent treatment by Clarke (1941) place sciadopa very close to E. ciniflonella. Meyrick stated that the species “probably belongs to the ciniflonella group”, which corresponds to Exaeretia, not Agonopterix. He described the forewing as having a white dot at the end of the cell, outlined in black (A. canadensis has a simple black spot in this position). Moreover, Clarke (1941) placed sciadopa in Martyrhilda (now a synonym of Exaeretia), and his figure of a sciadopa female is indistinguishable from D. ciniflonella; it is clearly not A. canadensis. Clarke considered sciadopa and klamathiana to be the New World counterparts of a Palaearctic concept of E. ciniflonella. Hodges' synonymy was made without comment.

NAME: quinquecristatella
author: Chambers
NOTE: NOTE: The taxon X. quinquecristatella was synonymized under X. aethiops by Meyrick (1925: 69) in his catalog of Gelechiidae, where these species were at the time placed in Telphusa. It is unknown on what basis Meyrick established the synonymy. This was followed by McDunnough in his 1939 checklist. Hodges (in Hodges et al. 1983) reinstated quinquecristatella as valid; this was followed by Lee & Brown (2008) but reversed to a junior synonym in the Lee et al. (2009) checklist. Thus as of the latest publication to treat the species, the current status is that quinquecristatella is regarded as a junior synonym. None of these works gave any explanation for the changes. The real identity of quinquecristatella remains uncertain. The TL is unknown. Chambers described the species in a paper in which there is a mixture of species from Bosque Co., TX and from KY, but for some species, such as quinquecristatella, he omitted to mention where it came from. The type appears to be lost. DNA barcoding and genitalia examination among Xenolechia species by JFL suggest that it is best to reinstate quinquecristatella as valid until a full revision is conducted.

Corro Chang & Metz (2021) used a cladistic analysis to clarify the unstable generic placement of the pestiferous Tuta absoluta (Meyrick, 1917) (not present in NA so far) and found that Phthorimaea, Tuta, and Scrobipalpuloides formed three separate groups with absoluta being part of a monophyletic Phthorimaea, whereas Tuta (with the extralimital atriplicella Kieffer & Jörgensen, 1910 as type species) constituted a separate clade, as did Scrobipalpuloides. As a result they recombined absoluta with Phthorimaea and reinstated Tuta as a separate, valid (extralimital) genus.

author: Lange

NAME: hoguei

author: Barnes & Lindsey

NAME: wrangeliensis
author: Zagulajev
NOTE: NOTE: The taxa wrangeliensis and albilobata have similar genitalia and DNA barcodes, including the sequenced holotype of wrangeliensis; wrangeliensis is hereby synonymized (n. syn.; contributed by JFL).

NAME: brucei
author: Fernald
NOTE: NOTE: The taxa H. brucei and its synonym chionastes are hereby transferred from Oidaematophorus to Hellinsia (n. comb.). Female genitalia lack the large “bell-shaped” antrum which Gielis (1993) used as a defining character for Oidaematophorus. The corpus bursae also has paired signa, which are absent in Oidamatophorus and irregularly present in Hellinsia. Male genitalia are similar to H. albilobata in having protruding distal apices of the sacculus of both valves.

NAME: linus
author: Barnes & Lindsey
NOTE: NOTE: Munroe (in Hodges et al. 1983) and Poole & Gentili (1996) used the Old World name H. lienigianus for this species.

NAME: philocremna
author: Meyrick
NOTE: NOTE: Synonymy by Gielis (1993).

NAME: angustus
author: Walsingham
NOTE: NOTE: Gielis (1993) synonymized both H. angustus and H. stramineus with H. pectodactylus. The Walsingham holotypes (NHMUK) represent two male genitalic forms which are herein raised back to species (rev. stat.). Given the variability seen in Palaearctic H. pectodactylus, more NA material should be examined to further assess variation between populations.

NAME: stramineus
author: Walsingham
NOTE: NOTE: See note under H. angustus.

NAME: poulini
author: Bigot
NOTE: NOTE: The name poulini (Bigot & Picard, 2005) is not available because the type repository was not indicated in the original publication. Bigot (2021) republished the description with the type repository included. The available name thus bears a different year and only one author. An image of the holotype genitalia (courtesy of Louis Handfield) is similar to the holotype of H. stramineus, and therefore poulini is transferred from Oidaematophorus to Hellinsia (n. comb.). Additional studies will determine whether or not H. poulini is indeed distinct from H. stramineus.

NAME: catalinae
author: Grinnell
NOTE: NOTE: Here transferred from Oidaematophorus to Hellinsia (n. comb.). Female genitalia lack the large “bell-shaped” antrum which Gielis (1993) used as a defining character for Oidaematophorus.

NAME: serenus
author: Meyrick
NOTE: NOTE: This species is herein reinstated as distinct from H. balanotes (rev. stat.) based on differences in wing maculation and male and female genitalia. Identified specimens are present in both the USNM and MGCL. Barnes & Lindsey (1921) illustrate an adult and male genitalia of a specimen that they indicate was identified by Meyrick via comparison with his type. Gielis (2003) synonymized H. serenus with H. balanotes without comment. Clarke (1955) lists H. serenus as a Meyrick type but did not indicate a repository. The current location of the type is unknown.

NAME: australis
author: Grinnell
NOTE: NOTE: Synonymized by Gielis (1993). Male genitalia of australis (originally described by Grinnell as a subspecies of H. subochraceus) and H. subochraceus are illustrated by Barnes & Lindsey (1921). These appear to represent two species with australis being more variable in the length of the left valve saccular process. However, australis is retained as a synonym here pending additional study.

NAME: devriesi
author: Landry & Gielis
NOTE: NEW NOTE: Added to the NA fauna based on a specimen collected in 2024 in FL (Halbert, in: Anderson & Hodges 2024a).

(2010)).

NOTE: NOTE: For many years this species has been referred to in NA and Europe as P. phoebus (described as Papilio phoebus by Fabricius, 1793), but that was based on a longstanding misidentification. That name applies to a species of the Altai Mountains in Asia. A different P. phoebus (described as Papilio phoebus by de Prunner, 1798) applies to the species of Europe and NA. However, the de Prunner name is a junior homonym of the Fabricius name so it is permanently unavailable. The oldest available name is P. corybas Fischer von Waldheim, 1823, and it has been applied recently to the NA species. A petition is currently before the ICZN to conserve the longstanding name Parnassius phoebus (Fabricius, 1793) for this species (Lukhtanov et al. 2019). Pending resolution of this matter, we retain the name P. phoebus (Fabricius, 1793).

NOTE: NOTE: This European species has been accidentally introduced to NA, but no persistent colonies have established (Pelham 2008).

NAME: arctica of authors
author: not Verity
NOTE: NOTE: This subspecies of the European species P. napi was reported in error from NA by Miller & Brown (1981).

NAME: napi of authors
author: not Linnaeus
NOTE: NOTE: This Old World name was widely used in the historical NA literature.

NAME: siblanca
author: Grishin
NOTE: NOTE: Described in Zhang et al. (2022d).

NAME: Miletinae
author: Reuter
NOTE: NOTE: The family-group name Miletinae (applied at various levels) has long been accepted as the proper name for this taxon, even though Gerydinae Doherty, 1886 is senior (ICZN Code Article 40).

NAME: hypophlaeas
author: Boisduval
NOTE: NOTE: Populations in NA were historically treated as subspecies of the Old World species L. phlaeas (Linnaeus), but were elevated to species status as L. hypophlaeas by Zhang et al. (2022d).

NAME: polaris of authors
author: not Courvoisier
NOTE: NOTE: Scott (1986) used this extralimital subspecies name based on a previous taxonomic arrangement; “true” L. phlaeas polaris is restricted to the Old World (Pelham 2008).

NAME: Alciphronia
author: Koçak
NOTE: NOTE: Zhang et al (2022d) determined that Alciphronia is a subgenus of Lycaena and that L. cupreus belongs to it.

NAME: tityrus
author: Poda
NOTE: NOTE: The record of L. hypoxanthe (Kirby) (a synonym of L. tityrus) from “Canada” by Barnes & Benjamin (1926) is based on a misidentification (Pelham 2008). L. tityrus is a European species.

NAME: Tharsalea
author: Scudder
NOTE: NOTE: This strictly New World group of coppers was defined by de Jong & van Dorp (2006) but they did not assign names. Zhang et al. (2020) confirmed this and employed Tharsalea as the senior name. Klots (1936) gave Tharsalea precedence over all other names as first reviser.

NAME: mariposa
author: Reakirt
NOTE: NOTE: The subspecies arrangement of Pyle & Hammond (2018) is followed here.

NAME: castro
author: Reakirt
NOTE: NOTE: ICZN (2010) Opinion 2261 designated a neotype for castro such that it represented T. helloides, and it is treated as such herein. It was considered a subspecies of T. dorcas by Pelham (2008), and a synonym of T. helloides in Pelham (2022). It was treated as a full species by Pohl et al. (2010), following Scott et al. (2006).

NAME: dorcas
author: Kirby
NOTE: NOTE: There is no consensus on relationships between taxa in the Lycaena dorcas complex (e.g., Ferris 1977; Scott 1979, 2006, 2008). The taxon florus was considered a subspecies of T. dorcas by Pelham (2008) and that is maintained provisionally herein pending further research. It seems clear that “florus” is not conspecific with dorcas but not at all clear that helloides and florus are different species despite reports of sympatry.

NAME: Theclinae
author: Swainson
NOTE: NOTE: The family-group name Theclinae (applied at various levels) has long been accepted as the proper name for this taxon, even though Zephyrinae Billberg, 1820 is senior.

NAME: Hypaurotis
author: Scudder
NOTE: NOTE: Zhang et al. (2020) synomized Habrodais and four Palaearctic genera under Hypaurotis, giving the latter priority over Habrodais as first reviser. However, that synonomy was premature as there are over a dozen related Palaearctic genera unexamined. The matter awaits further research and we retain Habrodais as a distinct genus.

NAME: Habrodais
author: Scudder
NOTE: NOTE: See note under Hypaurotis.

NAME: Eumaeini
author: Doubleday
NOTE: NOTE: Subtribe classification follows Robbins et al. (2022).

NAME: amyntor of authors
author: not Cramer
NOTE: NOTE: A record of C. amyntor from TX, which was the basis for inclusion of that species in the NA fauna by Poole & Gentili (1996), has been redetermined as C. herodotus (Pelham 2008).

NAME: longula
author: Hewitson
NOTE: NOTE: This species has been reported from AZ and TX based on sight records, and listed by Poole & Gentili (1996), but no verified NA records are known. Additionally, the synonym pastor was reported from NA by Barnes & McDunnough (1913). C. longula was excluded from the NA fauna by Pelham (2008).

NAME: Callophrys
author: Billberg
NOTE: NOTE: Zhang et al. (2021) reviewed this genus and proposed several genus level changes. These are adopted herein.

NAME: millerorum
author: Clench
NOTE: NOTE: One specimen of this taxon was recorded from Otero County, NM, by Johnson (1985). It is unclear whether this represents a stray into the USA, or an extreme of the local range of individual variation.

NAME: loki
author: Skinner
NOTE: NOTE: Pratt et al. (2011) united loki and thornei as conspecific.

NAME: viridis
author: Edwards
NOTE: NOTE: Treated as a synonym of C. dumetorum by Pelham (2008) but recognized as a full species by Pelham (2022).

NAME: perplexa
author: Barnes & Benjamin
NOTE: NOTE: The taxon perplexa was described as a race of C. dumetorum. Emmel et al. (in Emmel 1998) designated a lectotype for Thecla dumetorum. This lectotype represented a specimen of what had traditionally been considered Callophrys viridis. This created an uneasy juggling of names and the potential for further problems since the names dumetorum and viridis are both senior to sheridanii. ICZN (2021) Opinion 2291 resolved these by designating a neotype such that the name dumetorum is employed as it was before 1998 and gave sheridanii precedence over viridis if they are considered conspecific.

NAME: fulvescens
author: Edwards
NOTE: NOTE: Recent synonymy by Davenport (2018).

NAME: Phaeostrymon
author: Clench
NOTE: NOTE: Recent synonymy by Zhang et al. (2019b).

NAME: dryope

NAME: daraba

NAME: serapio

NAME: syllis

NOTE: NOTE: Recorded from TX by Bordelon (2009) and Rickard (2010).

NAME: angelia

NAME: ira
author: Hewitson
NOTE: NOTE: Reported from TX in the 2015 Season Summary of the Lepidopterists' Society (2016).

NAME: moctezuma

NAME: marsyas

NAME: toxea

NAME: isophthalma

NOTE: NOTE: This extralimital subspecies was listed as a valid NA species by Miller & Brown (in Hodges et al. 1983).

NAME: strabo

NAME: boeticus

NAME: battoides
author: Behr

NAME: allyni

NAME: xerces
author: Boisduval

author: Stradomsky

NAME: echo
author: Edwards
NOTE: NOTE: The inclusion of nigrescens, sidara, and cinerea as subspecies of C. echo is tentative, since some or all of these may be species-level taxa.

NAME: argiolus of authors
author: not Linnaeus
NOTE: NOTE: Reported from NA based on a previous taxonomic concept. “True” C. argiolus is restricted to the Old World (Pelham 2008).

NAME: gozora
author: Boisduval
NOTE: NOTE: Reported from NA as a subspecies of C. ladon by Miller & Brown (in Hodges et al. 1983), and subsequently recognized as a full species. The status of this taxon is unresolved and it was considered extralimital by (Pelham 2008).

NAME: neglectamajor

NAME: maritima
author: Leblanc
NOTE: NOTE: This taxon, historically treated as a subspecies, was convincingly designated a nomen nudum by Calhoun (2022).

NAME: ammon
author: Lucas
NOTE: NOTE: This species was first confirmed in NA from FL in 1985, and has since become established in the Lower Keys. It had been recorded previously from FL, but those previous reports were misidentifications of C. thomasi bethunebakeri; see Calhoun et al. (2002).

NAME: hanno of authors
author: not Stoll
NOTE: NOTE: H. ceraunus and all its subspecies were placed within a taxonomic concept of H. hanno by Lamas (2004), but H. ceraunus is treated here as a separate species, following Pelham (2008). Under the current concept, C. hanno is restricted to Central and South America.

NAME: lupini
author: Boisduval
NOTE: NOTE: The arrangement of taxa under this species is tentative; some of these may represent species-level taxa.

NAME: chlorina
author: Skinner
NOTE: NOTE: Treated as a distinct species by Davenport (2018).

NAME: monticola
author: Clemence
NOTE: NOTE: Treated as a distinct species by Davenport (2018).

NAME: dedeckera
author: Emmel, Emmel & Mattoon
NOTE: NOTE: Treated as a distinct species by Davenport (2018).

NAME: cotundra
author: Scott & Fisher
NOTE: NOTE: Opler (in Fisher 2009) elevated this taxon to the species level.

NAME: glandon
author: de Prunner
NOTE: NOTE: In the last half century the names glandon, aquilo, franklinii and rustica have all been applied at the species level to some or all populations of this complex in NA (e.g., Miller & Brown 1981; Ferris 1989; Opler 1992, 1999). Since no thorough analysis of NA populations has yet been presented, the following arrangement is tentative. It is unclear whether or not the name aquilo should be applied to the NA fauna. Until a lectotype or neotype for aquilo is designated, this issue will remain problematic but it is tentatively considered an Old World taxon herein.

NAME: argyrognomon of authors
author: not Bergstrasser
NOTE: NOTE: This Palaearctic name has been applied to NA populations under a previous taxonomic concept. As currently recognized, P. argyrognomon is restricted to the Old World.

NAME: samuelis
author: Nabokov
NOTE: NOTE: Lane & Weller (1994) offered support for the specific status of this taxon. Lucas et al. (2008) also supported this status, which we follow here. However, Packer et al. (1998) and Gompert et al. (2006) offer contrary evidence that it is a subspecies of Plebejus melissa.

NAME: icarus
author: Rottemburg
NOTE: NOTE: Introduced from Europe to NA, discovered in 2007 in QC (Hall 2007). Most of the Palaearctic synonymy is not included.

NAME: Riodinidae
author: Grote
NOTE: NOTE: ICZN (1977) Opinion 1073 placed Riodinidae (with the date as given) on the Official List of Family-group Names in Zoology as name no. 484 and placed Riodina Westwood, 1851 on the Official List of Generic Names in Zoology as name no. 2039.

NAME: sergia
author: Godman & Salvin
NOTE: NOTE: Excluded from the NA fauna by Pelham (2008); the synonym abreas was described from material mislabeled as being from AZ.

NAME: Riodininae
author: Grote
NOTE: NOTE: The tribal arrangement follows Zhang et al. (2019a).

NAME: domitianus of authors
author: not Fabricius
NOTE: NOTE: The report of this species from TX by De Vries (1997) is assumed to be a misidentification of C. ino (Pelham 2008).

NAME: Baeotis
author: Hübner
NOTE: NOTE: Zhang et al. (2021) determined that Colaciticus is a synonym of this genus, and that is adopted herein.

NAME: zonata
author: Felder
NOTE: NOTE: Reported from AZ by Saba & Winslow (2009).

NAME: nilus of authors
author: not Felder & Felder
NOTE: NOTE: Scott (1986) and Opler (1999) used the name C. nilus as the valid name for C. perditalis, but herein we treat NA populations under the latter name.

NAME: dreisbachi
author: McAlpine
NOTE: NOTE: Part of the type material for this species was stated to be from AZ, but the identity of that material is uncertain, and the species was excluded from the NA fauna by Pelham (2008).

NAME: argyrodines of authors
author: not Bates
NOTE: NOTE: Prior to the description of C. freemani in 1971, historical reports in NA referred to this species as C. argyrodines.

NAME: sinaloensis
author: McAlpine
NOTE: NOTE: This species was reported from TX, as subspecies nuevoleon by Durden (1982, 1990), but that record requires verification and it was excluded from the NA fauna by Pelham (2008).

NAME: narses of authors
author: not Staudinger
NOTE: NOTE: This name, a synonym of L. agesilas (Latreille, 1809), was used by Barnes & McDunnough (1913) prior to the description of L. sula peninsularis. L. agesilas does not occur in NA.

NAME: sessilis of authors
author: not Schaus
NOTE: NOTE: This name was used by Stallings & Turner (1946) prior to the description of L. sula peninsularis. It does not occur in NA (Pelham 2008).

NAME: emesia
author: Hewitson
NOTE: NOTE: Genus assignment by Zhang et al. (2019a).

NAME: Plesioarida
author: Trujano & García
NOTE: NOTE: Synonymy of Pleasioarida by Zhang et al. (2020).

NAME: mormo
author: Felder & Felder
NOTE: NOTE: Several recent authors (e.g., Forbes 1979; Pratt & Balmer 1991) strongly suggest that this complex, previously considered a single species, includes multiple species-level taxa. However, at this time there is no consensus on species-level boundaries. The arrangement presented here is partly based on studies cited above, as well as Opler & Warren (2002) and Davenport (2004a, 2004b, 2014, 2018), and is tentative.

NAME: hypoglauca
author: Godman & Salvin
NOTE: NOTE: Reported from NA by Glassberg (1999) but its occurrence here has not been verified and it was excluded from the NA fauna by Pelham (2008).

author: Barnes & Benjamin

NAME: lilis
author: Doubleday
NOTE: NOTE: This species was reported as a new NA (TX) record, as subspecies imitata, in the 2008 Season Summary of the Lepidopterists' Society (2009). It may have been intentionally released in the USA, and it is treated here as an unestablished introduction. It was excluded from the NA fauna by Pelham (2008, 2022).

NAME: cotytto
author: Guérin-Méneville
NOTE: NOTE: This species was reported as a new NA (TX) record, by Bordelon & Knudson (2006). It may have been intentionally released in the USA, and it is treated here as an unestablished introduction. It was excluded from the NA fauna by Pelham (2008, 2022).

NAME: polissena
author: Hewitson
NOTE: NOTE: Reports of this species (subspecies umbrana) from TX have not been verified, and the species was excluded from the NA fauna by Pelham (2008, 2022).

NAME: morgane
author: Geyer
NOTE: NOTE: This species was reported as a new NA (TX) record, by Bordelon & Knudson (2006). It may have been intentionally released in the USA, and it is treated here as an unestablished introduction. It was excluded from the NA fauna by Pelham (2008, 2022).

NAME: iphianassa
author: Doubleday
NOTE: NOTE: NA records of this species as well as the subspecies anaphissa and panamensis are erroneous. They are based on the TL for the synonym negreta, listed in error as “Los Angeles, California”. This species is restricted to South America (Pelham 2008).

NAME: cleobaea

NAME: nigrippus
author: Haensch

author: Godart

NAME: jamaicensis
author: Bates

NAME: carteri

NAME: juno

NAME: napaea of authors

NAME: euphrosyne

NAME: titania of authors

NAME: dia

author: Packard

The taxon rampartensis (n. syn.) is here treated as a synonym rather than a subspecies.

However, Quadrina and Caloecia form part of a New World group of “unusually large Lasiocampinae” closely related to Dendrolimus Germar, 1812 of Asia (Regier et al. 2000), the latter placed in Pinarini by Zolotuhin et al. (2012). Furthermore, Dendrolimus and the New World genera share a gregarious larval habit and winter diapause in the larval stage. Caloecia, Quadrina, Dicogaster, and Gloveria are therefore placed in Pinarini along with Dendrolimus.

NAME: cynthia
author: Drury

It escaped captivity in various localities over the past century, but only maintains viable wild populations in isolated areas in the eastern USA. It is known in Canada from a specimen in the MMMN collected at London, ON by Norman Criddle in 1905, and from a specimen in the ROM from downtown Toronto, ON. It may well have established temporary populations in these places, but it is deemed to be extirpated in Canada.

author: Benjamin

Morphological evidence supports the recognition of R. forbesi (and other subspecies) as a valid species as well (Zapata 2009).

Although the modal phenotype does differ among geographic regions, multiple phenotypes matching different taxa are often present at a single location. In addition, neither DNA barcodes nor genitalic morphology are diagnostic for the taxa previously recognized as species, and montanata, simsata, magnoliatoidata, and canavestita are hereby placed into synonymy under a single species, L. nivigerata (n. syn.), along with nocticolata (rev. syn.), which was previously synonymized with montanata.

NAME: Nasusina
author: Pearsall
NOTE: NOTE: As discussed by Barnes & McDunnough (1918b) and McDunnough (1949b), there are no unique morphological characters that unite all species within Nausina or within Prorella. They are distinguished from Eupithecia primarily on the presence of a rounded, bulging frons in Nasusina, and a projecting or pointed frons in Prorella (but absent in at least one species). Structurally similar modifications of the frons are found across a wide range of desert-dwelling Lepidoptera (e.g., Pyralidae, Noctuidae), and it is thought that this is an adaptation that aids in pupal emergence from hardened soil or plant substrates. When all other characters, including genitalic and external morphology and DNA barcode variation are considered, the species of Prorella and Nasusina (endemic to NA) fall squarely within Eupithecia, as McDunnough (1949b) suspected. Both genera are therefore placed into synonymy under Eupithecia (n. syn.).

NAME: Rheumaptera
author: Hübner
NOTE: NOTE: Traditionally (e.g., Ferguson, in: Hodges et al. 1983), Coryphista and Hydria have been treated as separate genera, but Scoble (1999) treated them as synonyms of Rheumaptera. Although Hausmann & Viidalepp (2012) provided a more restricted concept of Rheumaptera by maintaining Hydria as a valid genus, that is strongly contradicted by the Brehm et al. (2019) analysis. The multi-gene phylogenetic analysis of the latter demonstrated that the type species of Hydria (H. undulata) is embedded well within Rheumaptera — in fact, it comes out as sister to R. hastata, the type-species of Rheumaptera. Brehm et al. (2019) also presented a convincing argument that Coryphista is indeed a junior synonym of Rheumaptera. We follow Scoble (1999) and Brehm et al. (2019) and treat Coryphista and Hydria as junior synonyms of Rheumaptera.

NAME: metanemaria
author: Hulst

However, molecular data confirm a close relationship between metanemaria and marcescaria. Furthermore, metanemaria feeds on Baccharis spp. (Asteraceae), as do species of the varadaria group, the only macariines known to do so (Ferguson 2008). The monotypic genus Letispe (type species: metanemaria) is therefore placed into synonymy with Macaria (n. syn.), and its constituent taxa metanemaria and its synonym castalia are transferred to Macaria (n. comb.).

No subspecies are therefore recognized herein, pending review of the group.

(2011) resolved Selenia as forming a strongly supported sister group to Cepphis. Until the tribal classification of the Anagogini-group is resolved we maintain usage of the previous concept for NA Anagogini (McGuffin 1987), but remove Metarranthis, Cepphis, Slossonia, and Selenia to uncertain tribal placement (near Palyadini) following Brehm et al. NOTE: NOTE: This unnamed species refers to TX populations previously attributed to V. marginata by Schmidt et al. (2018). The Neotropical taxon V. marginata, described from the highlands of Guatemala, was raised from synonymy with V. rubicundaria by Ferguson & Opler (2006), based on uncertain identification of USA specimens of unspecified provenance. Possibly, Ferguson believed the name to apply to a species found in the White Mountains of AZ, to which it is most similar. However, due to the uncertain application of this name to any NA species, V. marginata was not included as part of the NA fauna by Schmidt & Opler (2008). Zaspel et al. (2008) subsequently applied the name to the AZ-NM species, but Lafontaine & Schmidt (2010) disagreed and listed that taxon as “Virbia near marginata”. More recently, the name marginata was applied to the aurantiaca-group populations of south TX (Schmidt et al. 2018), but further study has shown that this is also wrong (BCS, in prep.) and that both NA taxa that the name marginata has been applied to are likely undescribed species. “True” V. marginata does not occur in NA. NAME: Oxycnemis
author: Grote
NOTE: NOTE: Systematic placement follows Keegan et al. (2019). The genus Oxycnemis is a paraphyletic assemblage of species that require assignment to several genera in two different subfamilies, Amphipyrinae and Oncocnemidinae (Keegan et al. 2019). The type-species O. advena was placed in Amphipyrinae, thereby associating “true” Oxycnemis with Amphipyrinae: Psaphidini, whereas “Oxycnemis” gracillinea was placed in Oncocnemidinae by Keegan et al. (2019). Based on morphological and DNA barcode similarity of the remaining Oxycnemis species to those analyzed by Keegan et al. (2019), Oxycnemis fusimacula is retained within “true” Oxycnemis, and grandimacula is placed in “Oxycnemis” in the broad sense (Amphipyrinae); acuna is closely related to gracillinea. To avoid the confusion of two “Oxycnemis” genus concepts in two unrelated subfamilies, the Oncocnemidinae species formerly in Oxycnemis are here provisionally transferred to Sympistis, i.e. Sympistis acuna n. comb. and Sympistis gracillinea n. comb. The latter two species are indeed closely related to NA Sympistis, although the limits of that genus also requires reassessment.

NAME: Catabenoides
author: Poole
NOTE: NOTE: In his revision of Catabenoides, Becker (2021) revised the concept of C. divisa (Moeschler) from junior synonymy under C. vitrina to senior synonymy of C. insularis Troubridge. However, some significant taxonomic discrepancies arise with Becker’s revised taxon concepts. Foremost, all NA populations were assigned to two widespread species by Becker (2021), but DNA barcode variation indicates that there are likely four or more (see public BOLD data). Furthermore, the FL taxon insularis was described as distinct from other NA taxa, also borne out by DNA barcodes, and therefore cannot be a widespread NA – Antillean species (C. divisa sensu Becker 2021). Another problem is the synonymy of insularis under divisa as proposed by Becker (2021). Troubridge (2020) expressly states that a diagnostic trait of insularis is the lack of a black longitudinal forewing streak in females, yet the holotype female of insularis is described by Möschler as having the streak. Consequently, we maintain prior taxonomic concepts of the NA Catabenoides until these issues can be addressed.

NAME: Lithophane
author: Hübner
ID INFO: ID INFO (partial): Covell & Metzler (1992), Metzler (1998), Webster & Thomas (1999), Troubridge & Lafontaine (2003), Troubridge (2006b, 2020), Brou & Lafontaine (2009), Walsh (2009).
NOTE: NEW NOTE: Troubridge & Lafontaine (2003) list the members of some sections and groups, but they are not delimited sufficiently to construct a complete classification of the genus, so we do not formally recognize any sections or species groups in Lithophane. Troubridge & Lafontaine (2003) reviewed the "lepida species group/complex", and state that Lithophane species were arranged into three groupings or "sections" by Forbes (1954). However, Forbes (1954) did not designate any formal groups, simply listing species below abbreviated summaries of character states from his key.

NAME: lamda
author: Fabricius
NOTE: NOTE: Reports of this species in NA refer to L. fagina and L. thaxteri; L. lamda is strictly Palaearctic (Forbes 1954 listed both thaxteri and fagina as races of L. lambda).

NAME: adipel
author: Benjamin
NOTE: NOTE: The taxon adipel was treated as a subspecies of lepida in a revision of the Lithophane lepida group by Troubridge & Lafontaine (2003). In Lafontaine & Schmidt (2010) adipel was raised to species without further comment. The two taxa, both based on eastern NA type specimens, represent slightly different adult phenotypes that differ in geographic range and possibly larval hostplant, as detailed in Schweitzer et al. (2011) and Wagner et al. (2011). The information presented in the latter two references, in addition to novel DNA barcode data (BCS unpublished data), do not provide compelling evidence that lepida and adipel represent separate species, and adipel is accordingly returned to subspecies status here.

NAME: moffatiana
author: Grote
NOTE: NOTE: A previously unrecognized species of Pyreferra, the biology of which is discussed by Wagner et al. (2011), has been included within the concept of P. citrombra. Examination of the type specimens of Pyreferra junior synonyms reveals that the name moffatiana applies to this taxon, and is here raised to species status (rev. stat.). Pyreferra moffatiana is externally intermediate between P. hesperidago and P. citrombra, being larger than P. citrombra but with more curved forewing lines; compared to P. hesperidago it is paler overall with a less sinuate medial line. Based on DNA barcodes, the nearest relative is P. citrombra which differs by about 3%.

author: Guenée
NOTE: NOTE: The description of this species is based on an Abbott painting, and cannot be identified with certainty. It was listed twice by Franclemont & Todd (in Hodges et al. 1983), in Sericaglaea (MONA No. 9940) and in error in Rhynchagrotis (MONA No. 11044).

NAME: decipiens
author: Grote
NOTE: NOTE: The western NA species is currently known as S. decipiens, but that name may not be correct. Franclemont (in Forbes 1954) treated decipiens as a form of S. bicolorago and returned acta to full species, which may be the correct arrangement. The type locality of decipiens was purportedly IL, but the type specimen appears to be lost so a neotype is needed to resolve this issue. Franclemont & Todd (in Hodges et al. 1983) subsequently treated decipiens as a full species with acta as a synonym but without explanation. Herein we retain the latter interpretation pending taxonomic work.

NAME: intexta

NAME: Trichopolia
author: Grote
NOTE: NOTE: Trichopolia dentatella, the type species of Trichopolia, is very similar in antennal and genitalic morphology and wing phenotype to Protorthodes antennata (Jan Metlevski, pers. comm.), and DNA barcode variation confirms a close relationship between these two taxa and the remainder of Protorthodes, including the type species Protorthodes curtica. Similarly, Trichopolia suspicionis is most closely related to Protorthodes alfkeni. When McDunnough (1943) described Protorthodes, he made no mention of Trichopolia, apparently an oversight on his part. The type species of the two genera are here treated as congeners, rendering Protorthodes a junior subjective synonym of Trichopolia (n. syn.) and resulting in the following new combinations: Trichopolia curtica (n. comb.), T. eureka (n. comb.), T. incincta (n. comb.), T. argentoppida (n. comb.), T. mulina (n. comb.), T. oviduca (n. comb.), T. orobia (n. comb.), T. melanopis (n. comb.), T. texicana (n. comb.), T. perforata (n. comb.), T. rufula (n. comb.), T. ustulata (n. comb.), T. alfkenii (n. comb.), T. antennata (n. comb.).
